email.scenario: You are taking Professor Grant's environmental science course. You were sick and missed last week's lab session, in which students collected water samples. The lab report is due next Monday.
points: Explain why you missed the lab
Ask whether you can make up the session or use another student's data
Request an extension if necessary
email.model:
Dear Professor Grant,

I hope you are doing well. I am writing because I missed last Thursday's lab session. I had a high fever and was advised by the campus clinic to stay home, and I can provide a note from the clinic if needed.

I understand that the water samples collected in that session are essential for the lab report. Would it be possible for me to make up the session at another time? If that is not practical, could I use data collected by one of my classmates instead?

In either case, I may need a few extra days to complete the report properly. Would you consider extending my deadline to Thursday?

Thank you for your understanding.

Best regards,
Kenji Sato

discussion.professor: Many universities now record their lectures and post them online. Some educators believe this helps students learn, while others worry that it reduces attendance and engagement. In your opinion, should universities make recordings of all lectures available to students? Why or why not?

students.name: Daniel
students.text: I think recordings are essential. Students who work part-time or have health problems sometimes can't attend, and recordings give them an equal chance to keep up. I also rewatch difficult parts before exams.

students.name: Sofia
students.text: I'm not convinced. When I know a lecture is recorded, I'm tempted to skip it, and I never actually find time to watch it later. Being in the room forces me to pay attention and ask questions.

discussion.model: I understand Sofia's concern about motivation, but I agree with Daniel that universities should provide recordings. The key point, in my view, is that recordings are a supplement rather than a replacement for attending. For example, in my statistics class last year, I attended every lecture but still struggled with some proofs. Being able to pause the recording and go through each step at my own pace helped me far more than my notes did. As for the attendance problem, professors could simply make in-class activities, such as short quizzes or group discussions, part of the final grade. That way, students would still have a clear reason to come to class, while those who genuinely cannot attend would not fall behind.

discussion.professor: Some cities have started to ban private cars from their downtown areas, allowing only pedestrians, bicycles, and public transportation. Supporters say this makes city centers cleaner and safer. Critics argue that it hurts local businesses and makes life harder for some residents. Do you think banning cars from downtown areas is a good idea? Explain your view.

students.name: Ryan
students.text: I support it. Cities that have done this have less air pollution and fewer traffic accidents. People also spend more time walking around and shopping, which can actually help businesses.

students.name: Mei
students.text: It sounds nice, but it isn't fair to everyone. Elderly people and people with disabilities may depend on cars, and delivery companies need access to stores too.

discussion.model: Both Ryan and Mei raise valid points, but I believe a partial ban is more realistic than a complete one. Mei is right that some people truly depend on cars, so a city could still allow access for residents with disabilities, taxis, and delivery vehicles during certain hours, such as early in the morning. At the same time, ordinary private cars could be kept out during the day. What neither of my classmates mentioned is the importance of reliable public transportation. A ban only works if people have a convenient alternative. If a city invests in frequent buses and safe bike lanes before introducing restrictions, residents are much more likely to accept the change and continue visiting downtown shops.

discussion.professor: Some universities require all students to complete a certain number of hours of community service before they graduate. Supporters say this teaches responsibility and connects students to their communities. Others believe volunteering should be a personal choice. Should universities make community service a graduation requirement? Why or why not?

students.name: Olivia
students.text: I think it should be required. Many students would never volunteer otherwise, but once they try it, they often discover causes they care about. My high school required it, and I still volunteer at an animal shelter.

students.name: Marcus
students.text: I disagree. Forced volunteering isn't really volunteering. Students who are made to do it may just try to finish the hours as quickly as possible, which doesn't help anyone.

discussion.model: I understand Marcus's point, but I agree with Olivia that a requirement can be valuable, as long as it is designed well. The problem Marcus describes happens mainly when students are simply told to collect hours. If universities instead connected service to students' majors, the experience would feel meaningful rather than forced. For instance, education majors could tutor children at local schools, and accounting students could help low-income families with their tax forms. In that case, students would not only help their communities but also gain practical experience that is directly useful for their future careers. In my view, the real question is not whether to require service, but how to make it relevant enough that students take it seriously.

discussion.professor: Since 2020, many companies have allowed employees to work from home some or all of the time. Some managers believe that remote work increases productivity, while others think that it weakens teamwork and creativity. In your opinion, is remote work better or worse for companies in the long term?

students.name: Hannah
students.text: Remote work is better. Employees save hours of commuting time, and many people concentrate better at home without office distractions. Companies can also save money on office space.

students.name: Raj
students.text: I think it's worse in the long run. New employees learn a lot by watching experienced colleagues, and that's hard to do over video calls. Spontaneous conversations also lead to new ideas.

discussion.model: Both Hannah and Raj make strong arguments, but I believe a hybrid model is the best long-term solution. Hannah is right that focused tasks, such as writing reports or analyzing data, are often done more efficiently at home. However, I share Raj's concern about new employees. When I worked as an intern last summer, I learned most of my practical skills by listening to how my supervisor handled phone calls and solved problems, something I could never have learned remotely. Therefore, companies could ask employees to come to the office two or three days a week for meetings, training, and collaborative work, while allowing them to stay home on other days. This approach would keep the productivity benefits of remote work without losing the learning that happens face to face.

discussion.professor: Plastic waste is a growing problem in oceans and landfills. Some people argue that individuals should take responsibility by changing their shopping habits, while others say that governments and companies must lead the way through laws and new technology. Who should play the main role in reducing plastic waste? Explain your view.

students.name: Grace
students.text: Individuals need to change first. If consumers stop buying products wrapped in plastic, companies will have no choice but to change their packaging.

students.name: Diego
students.text: That's unrealistic. Most people are busy and just buy what's available. Governments need to ban single-use plastics and make companies pay for the waste they create.

discussion.model: In my view, governments should take the leading role, although individuals still matter. I agree with Diego that it is unrealistic to expect millions of consumers to change their habits on their own, especially when plastic-free options are often more expensive or harder to find. However, Grace raises an important point about consumer pressure, and I think the two approaches work best together. A good example is the plastic bag fee introduced in many countries. The law itself was a government decision, but its success depended on shoppers changing a daily habit, such as carrying reusable bags. Once that habit became normal, people began to support even stricter rules. So governments should create the framework, and individual choices can then reinforce it.

discussion.professor: Some educators have proposed replacing traditional letter grades with a simple pass/fail system, especially for first-year university courses. They argue that this reduces stress and encourages students to explore new subjects. Others worry that students will put in less effort. What is your opinion? Should first-year courses be graded pass/fail?

students.name: Emma
students.text: Yes. First-year students are adjusting to a new environment, and pass/fail grading would let them take challenging courses outside their major without worrying about their GPA.

students.name: Kenji
students.text: No. Grades give useful feedback. If I only knew I had passed, I wouldn't know whether I had really mastered the material or just barely made it.

discussion.model: I think a pass/fail system is a good idea for first-year courses, but only if it is combined with detailed feedback. Emma is right that fear of a low grade often stops students from exploring unfamiliar subjects. For example, a friend of mine was interested in philosophy but chose an easier course instead because she was afraid of lowering her GPA. At the same time, Kenji makes a valid point that students need to know how well they understand the material. Professors could solve this by giving written comments or scores on individual assignments, while recording only pass or fail on the official transcript. That way, students would still receive the information they need to improve, but they would feel free to take intellectual risks during their first year.

discussion.professor: Research on the effects of social media on young people's mental health has produced mixed results. Some lawmakers have proposed limiting the amount of time teenagers can spend on social media apps each day. Do you think such limits are a good idea? Why or why not?

students.name: Sophie
students.text: I support time limits. Many teenagers stay up late scrolling, which hurts their sleep and their schoolwork. A daily limit would help them build healthier habits.

students.name: Ahmed
students.text: I don't think limits will work. Teenagers will just find ways around them, like using a parent's account. It would be better to teach them how to use social media wisely.

discussion.model: I agree with Ahmed that legal time limits are not the best solution, although I understand Sophie's concern about sleep. The main problem with a strict limit is that it treats all social media use as equally harmful. In reality, some teenagers use these apps to stay in touch with distant relatives or to join communities related to their hobbies, which can actually improve their well-being. What matters more is how and when they use them. Instead of a daily limit, schools could teach students to recognize warning signs, such as comparing themselves constantly with others. In addition, apps could be required to turn off notifications late at night by default. This would address the sleep problem Sophie mentioned without taking away the benefits of staying connected.

discussion.professor: Many national museums charge admission fees to cover their costs. Some people argue that museums should be free to everyone and funded entirely by taxes, since they preserve a shared cultural heritage. Others believe visitors should pay for what they use. Should public museums be free? Explain your opinion.

students.name: Lucas
students.text: Museums should be free. Culture belongs to everyone, and fees discourage low-income families from visiting. When some museums in the UK became free, the number of visitors increased dramatically.

students.name: Yuna
students.text: I don't think they should be completely free. Taxes are limited, and not everyone visits museums. It seems fairer for visitors to pay at least part of the cost.

discussion.model: In my opinion, public museums should be free for residents, while tourists could be asked to pay a fee. Lucas makes an important point that admission fees discourage families with limited budgets, and these are often the children who would benefit most from exposure to art and history. On the other hand, I understand Yuna's concern about fairness to taxpayers. A two-level system would address both issues. Residents, who already support museums through their taxes, could enter for free, whereas international visitors, who do not contribute to local taxes, would pay an entrance fee. Several museums already use similar systems, and the income from tourists can be used to maintain collections and develop educational programs for local schools.
